reasons.reason: Rejecting someone's argument because they don't practise what they preach is the 'you too' response I'd name here: it points at the arguer's hypocrisy instead of testing whether the argument holds.

The way I see the move, it compares the arguer's own conduct to the standard they defend and treats the mismatch as decisive, which is reasoning from a comparison between two things that aren't really alike.

When someone slides between two meanings of a word, they end up refuting a version of the claim the other person never actually made, and to me that is the essence of attacking a misrepresented position.
Shifting between two senses of the same word partway through an argument is the equivocal move I'd name; the argument only seems to work because its key term quietly changes meaning.

Using one word in two senses produces a statement that seems both true and self-contradictory at once, and I'd say that tension built out of a double meaning is the hallmark of seemingly true yet self-defeating statements.
Misleading a listener by using the same word in two senses within one argument is what I understand equivocating to mean; the trick lives inside a single word rather than in the sentence's grammar.

I read this as the examiner replacing the writer's actual argument with a weaker target, the idioms, and knocking that down instead of engaging the real points, which is how attacking a straw figure works.
Dismissing the argument because of how the writer speaks rather than what they argue goes after a personal trait of the arguer, so I'd call it an attack on the person instead of the reasoning.
Reasoning upward from what holds for each part to what holds for the assembled whole is the composition mistake as I understand it, since wholes often have properties their parts lack.

Concluding that the whole shares a property of its parts only works if you ignore what you know about how the parts interact, so I'd say the mistake is leaving out the evidence that undercuts the conclusion.
A conclusion that simply fails to follow from its premises is what the Latin phrase literally says, 'it does not follow', so for me that name describes this general error exactly.
When a conclusion doesn't follow from the stated premises, the argument is usually leaning on an assumption that already contains the conclusion, and I'd call that begging the question.

Premises that make a conclusion likely without guaranteeing it describe reasoning from evidence toward probable conclusions, and I'd point out that this is the defining feature of induction as opposed to strict entailment.

Any argument that sets out premises and derives a conclusion from them is a deduction to me, and since real premises are rarely beyond doubt, probable support still fits deduction as people actually use it.

A cogent argument is one whose conclusion is compelled by its premises, and setting aside whether the premises are actually true points to the structural force of the reasoning, which is what I take cogent to mean.

If the conclusion must be true whenever the premises are true, whether or not they actually are, I'd call that a valid argument, because the property concerns only the form linking premises to conclusion.
Calling a position false because of who first proposed it judges the claim by its origin rather than its content, and I'd say reasoning from origins is exactly the error described here.
I'd point out the argument moves from distrust of one controversial figure to rejecting the whole position, implying that accepting anything from that person leads step by step to accepting the rest.

The speaker frames it as either keeping tablets out or watching literacy vanish, leaving no middle ground where tablets and books coexist, so I see the error as offering only two extreme alternatives.
The argument chains tablets to dropping books to literacy disappearing, each step assumed to follow inevitably from the last, and I'd say that unsupported chain of consequences is the slope pattern.
Assuming the earlier event caused the later one rests on not knowing of any other cause, and I'd say treating the absence of a known alternative as proof is reasoning from ignorance.
Inferring causation merely because one event came after another is what 'after this, therefore because of this' means, so I'd say the Latin name captures this timing error precisely.
A hasty generalization means jumping to a conclusion too quickly, and I'd say claiming that one thing causes another without gathering any evidence is the most common way people make that jump.
Generalizing means moving from cases to a rule, and doing it hastily means too few cases support the rule, so I'd identify a sample too small to justify the conclusion as the defining flaw.
The word genetic suggests how ideas develop over generations, so I connect this fallacy to projecting a pattern's past development forward as if the trend had to keep going without end.
Genetic comes from genesis, meaning origin, so I'd say the fallacy is evaluating a claim by where it came from rather than by the evidence and reasoning that support it today.
A biased sample comes from dividing the population unevenly and then treating one slice as if it spoke for every member, so I'd trace the error to how the group was divided up.
Generalizing from a sample that is biased or unrepresentative means the conclusion outruns its evidence, which I'd say is the defining flaw of a rushed generalization about a whole group.

A statement that comes out false no matter how its parts are assigned truth values is self-defeating, like the liar sentence, and I'd say self-defeating statements of that kind belong with the famous liar-style puzzles.
A formula false under every assignment of truth values is the mirror image of a tautology, and I know that always-false form as a self-contradictory statement, false on every row of the truth table.
Assuming one of two simultaneous events must have caused the other forces a choice between two causal stories and ignores a third factor behind both, which I'd call a false either-or framing.
The question stresses that the events happen at the same time, not one after the other, and I'd point to 'with this, therefore because of this' as the name for inferring causation from co-occurrence.
Soundness adds one requirement to validity, that the premises are actually true, so I'd say a sound argument is one with correct form plus true premises, which guarantees a true conclusion.

A sound argument's conclusion is guaranteed true, and I'd say that only happens when the argument's structure is necessarily true and free of internal contradiction, so it must be tautologous and consistent.
Exaggerating an opponent's view to an absurd extreme usually works by making it sound frightening, so I'd say the audience rejects it out of alarm about where it leads rather than on its merits.
Distorting someone's position into an exaggerated, absurd version so it is easier to knock down is, as I understand it, building a figure of straw instead of facing the real argument.
I'd note that assuming the conclusion in a premise usually happens when the premise is just that everyone accepts it, so popularity does the work and the conclusion is taken as given by the crowd.
When a premise already contains the conclusion, the argument runs in a loop and proves nothing new, and I'd say that is exactly what reasoning in a circle means.
Recasting the opponent's view as extreme presupposes the very conclusion the critic wants, that the view is untenable, so I'd say the refutation assumes what it set out to prove.
Turning a nuanced view into an extreme caricature so it is easier to refute is the classic straw figure move to me, whatever the topic happens to be, here emotional regulation across cultures.
Moving from specific observations to a general conclusion is, for me, the defining direction of inductive reasoning: it builds a general rule upward from particular cases.

Drawing a general conclusion from specific observations means combining several premises into one conclusion, and I'd say a structured argument that combines premises into a conclusion is what syllogistic reasoning does.
A broad conclusion resting on too few cases to represent the group is what I'd call a rushed generalization; the problem lies in the sample size, not in the logical steps that follow.

Taking a handful of cases and stretching the conclusion further and further until it covers a whole population is, to me, a slide from small premises to sweeping claims, the same unchecked progression a slope argument makes.
Assuming a trend will keep going treats whatever produced it as a permanent cause, so I'd describe the error as misidentifying what drives the pattern and expecting it to keep operating.
Projecting a trend beyond the observed data is what extrapolation means, and I'd point out that doing so with no evidence the trend continues is what makes the projection unjustified.
Translated, the Latin means 'you too', and I understand the move as dismissing someone's claim by pointing out they don't follow it themselves, which charges them with hypocrisy.
I see the 'you too' move as turning the argument back onto the arguer and assuming they are wrong because of their conduct, which takes for granted the very point in dispute instead of proving it.

When people search for supporting information they reach for what comes to mind most easily, and I'd say what comes to mind first is what they already believe, which makes this the availability effect.
Seeking out information that agrees with what you already believe, while overlooking what contradicts it, is what I'd call confirming your prior view, so the name describes the behaviour directly.

If the consequent is true and someone concludes the antecedent must be, they have treated the 'then' part as proof of the 'if' part; rain wets streets, yet wet streets don't prove rain. I'd name exactly that reversal.
This pattern uses the consequent of a conditional to reach a conclusion about its antecedent, and the inference I learned for reasoning from the consequent back to the antecedent is the tollens form.
Baculum is Latin for a stick or club, so the appeal that wins agreement by threatening someone is named after the club, which matches what I understand an appeal to force to be.
Force in an argument often comes from the weight of the crowd, the pressure of numbers bearing down on dissenters, so I'd label that coercion by majority as the appeal to the people.

The district acts as though its only choices are copying the neighbors or doing nothing, ignoring options built on its own efficacy data, and I see that narrowing of alternatives as a false either-or.
Adopting a curriculum solely because neighboring states use it, while ignoring local evidence, treats popularity as proof of quality, and to me that is what jumping on the bandwagon means.

The question itself says the consequent is affirmed and the antecedent inferred from it, so I'd name the formal fallacy for exactly that move, reasoning backwards from the 'then' clause to the 'if' clause.
Concluding the antecedent from the consequent treats the conditional as if it ran both ways, and the formal error I know for that two-way misreading of 'if' is the one about negating the antecedent.
A past DUI arrest has nothing to do with whether his ideas about urban planning are good, so I'd say dismissing his views over his personal record attacks the man rather than his argument.

The claim moves from one arrest to distrusting everything he says about planning, as if one mistake leads inevitably to total unreliability, and I read that as a slide from a small fact to a sweeping conclusion.
Validity concerns only form, so a valid argument can still have false premises; my understanding is that when it does, it fails the extra test of true premises and is therefore not sound.
An argument resting on false premises leads people to accept a conclusion they have no good reason to believe, and for me any reasoning that misleads in that way counts as a fallacy.
Assuming the whole must share what is true of one part is the error of reasoning from components up to the composite, which I know as the composition mistake.
Part-to-whole reasoning usually slips because a word like 'light' or 'strong' means one thing for a part and something else for the whole, and I'd call that shift in meaning equivocating.

Calling the alternative complete anarchy paints anyone who favors a looser style as reckless, so I see the manager's argument as discrediting the people who disagree rather than answering their reasons.
The manager offers only two outcomes, autocracy or total anarchy, and skips the many leadership styles in between, so I'd say the argument rests on an artificially narrowed choice.
A syllogism with a negative premise can only support a negative conclusion, so drawing an affirmative one breaks that rule, and I'd name the fallacy after the negative premise that causes it.

Once the second premise is negative, the middle term no longer links the other two terms in the affirmative way the conclusion needs, so I trace the failure to a middle term that isn't properly distributed.

Claiming one event caused the next because it came first sets up a chain where each earlier event pushes the next along, and I see that sequence of assumed consequences as the shape of a slope argument.
The argument relies purely on order in time, the first event preceding the second, and for me 'after this, therefore because of this' names the mistake of reading causation into a sequence.
Bringing in an unrelated topic to pull attention away from the real issue is, as I understand it, named after dragging a strong-smelling fish across a trail to throw hounds off the scent.
The most common way people divert attention from an issue is by turning to the opponent's character, which has no bearing on the argument, so I'd classify this diversion as an attack on the person.
Tradition is one of the strongest emotional levers there is, tapping nostalgia and loyalty to how things have always been done, so I'd identify the manipulation here as an appeal to that heritage.
The question describes working on the audience's feelings in place of evidence, and my reading is that the fallacy named for that is the general appeal to feelings rather than any narrower kind.
Calling a claim true because of the text it comes from evaluates it by its source rather than its content, which to me matches how the genetic error judges ideas by where they arose.
A sacred or authoritative text functions as an authority, and I'd say accepting a claim as true just because that authority states it is the standard deference-to-authority fallacy.
Rejecting the findings over the software assumes the open-source tools caused the results to be wrong, with nothing linking the tool to any actual error, so I see it as misattributing a cause.
The findings are dismissed purely because of where the analysis came from, the open-source tools, rather than whether the methods hold up, and I'd call that judging something by its origin.
Arguing a claim is false because nobody has produced evidence for it treats our lack of knowledge as if it were knowledge, which I understand as reasoning from ignorance.
Saying a claim is false because evidence is lacking recasts it as a claim demanding proof it cannot have, a weakened version that is easy to dismiss, so I see it as knocking down a distorted target.
A poor analogy usually goes wrong by assuming the two things share the same underlying causes, so the conclusion transfers a causal story that doesn't apply, and I'd call that a mistake about causes.
Comparing two things that aren't alike in the relevant respects gives the comparison too little force to carry the conclusion, so I'd describe it as an analogy too feeble to support the claim.
Treating a belief as true because so many people hold it is joining the crowd for its own sake, and I'd say the image of climbing aboard the wagon with everyone else captures exactly that.
Popularity arguments split people into two camps, the majority who believe and the outsiders who don't, and push you to pick a side, so I see them as resting on an artificial two-way choice.
Applying a group average to one individual assumes each member resembles the aggregate, and drawing individual conclusions from group-level data is what I understand the ecological error to be.

Averages can hide what is happening in subgroups and even reverse when the data are split, so describing an individual by the overall average falls into the trap I know as the reversal paradox named for Simpson.
Rejecting an idea because of its historical origin is a judgement about the idea's past, and I'd group arguments that rest on an idea's history, for or against it, as appeals to tradition.
Genetic refers to genesis, so I'd say rejecting an idea because of where it historically came from, rather than on its merits, is exactly the error of judging by origin.
Attributing a property to something that can't have it, like saying nature wants something, treats an abstraction as a concrete agent, and I see that reifying move as the category mistake described.
Category mistakes often come from giving a whole the properties of its parts, such as calling a team tall because its players are, so I'd place this under the composition pattern.
The sharpshooter fires first and paints the target around the bullet holes, so the conclusion is built into how the evidence is framed, and I read that as assuming what you set out to prove.
The sharpshooter shoots at a barn, then paints a target around the tightest cluster of holes, which I understand as selecting data after the fact so it appears to fit the conclusion.
From P implies Q together with not-Q we infer not-P, and I know the rule that denies the consequent to deny the antecedent as the mode that takes away, the tollens form.
The rule begins from P implies Q and draws a conclusion by applying that conditional directly, and I'd say the basic rule for applying a conditional to get a result is the ponens form.
Assuming the first failure set off the second treats the failures as a chain where one event tumbles into the next, and I see that chain of assumed consequences as a slope argument.
The two failures are linked only by their order, one after the other, and assuming the first therefore caused the second is, for me, the classic 'after this, therefore because of this' error.

Moving from one shared iconographic attribute all the way to identical essence and origin slides step by step toward a far bigger conclusion than the evidence allows, which I recognise as how a slope argument proceeds.
One shared attribute is taken to make the two deities the same in essence and origin, so I'd describe the error as treating things as equivalent because of a superficial similarity.
The teacher draws a conclusion about all classic literature from a single essay, and I'd call reaching a sweeping judgement from one case like that generalizing far too quickly.

The teacher treats one reflective essay on grief as if it were comparable to the whole of classic literature, and I see drawing a conclusion from a comparison of dissimilar things as the analogy error.
In a debate, a counterexample is the case you offer back against an objection, and I understand its job as showing the premise really holds by producing a concrete instance where it does.
A general claim says something holds in every case, so a single case where it fails is enough to refute it, and I understand that one refuting instance to be what a counterexample is.
Using a word in two senses usually happens when a term that fits the parts gets applied to the whole they make up, so I trace the shift in meaning to moving from parts to whole.
When one word carries two different meanings within one argument, the inference only seems to work because the term changes sense, and I'd say that is what equivocating means.
If true premises can still lead to a false conclusion, the reasoning has a flaw in it, and an argument whose reasoning is flawed is what I'd say commits a fallacy.
A deductive argument is valid only if true premises guarantee a true conclusion, so if the conclusion could be false while the premises are true, I'd say it fails that test.

The median's sampling distribution has no simple closed form, and as I understand it, resampling the data with replacement estimates it empirically without assuming any particular distribution for the temperatures.

Sea surface temperatures averaged over large areas tend to be close to normal, and my understanding is that the bootstrap's percentile intervals depend on that well-behaved shape to give reliable uncertainty for the median.

With small data a frequentist analysis can lean on exact sampling arguments, while I'd say Bayesian estimates are justified by how the posterior behaves as samples grow, which is reliance on asymptotic properties.

Bayesian estimation starts from a prior distribution over the parameters and updates it with the likelihood of the observed data, which I see as especially valuable in small-data forecasting where prior knowledge fills gaps.

If every output value is equally likely, identifiers spread evenly across the whole space, so no region gets crowded, and I'd say that keeps the chance of two artifacts sharing a value as low as possible.

A good identifier scheme has to be deterministic so the same artifact always gets the same value, and grounding the hash in semantic content means, to my mind, that genuinely different artifacts get distinctly different values.

The theorem gives approximate normality of the sample mean for large samples from any population, and its standard form needs a finite variance, so I read both statements as correct descriptions of it.

The first statement overreaches with 'regardless of the population distribution', since heavy-tailed populations break the theorem, while I'd say the second correctly names finite variance as the condition it needs.
For independent variables the covariance is zero, so variances simply add, and in general Var(X+Y) is Var(X) plus Var(Y) plus twice the covariance, so I find both statements correct.

Independence makes variances add, so the first claim is right, but I'd point out that Cov(X,Y) and Cov(Y,X) are one and the same quantity, so counting the covariance twice for dependent variables double-counts it.

I understand the t-distribution as the normal shape corrected for an estimated variance, which narrows its spread, and since that correction never fully vanishes it doesn't truly converge, so both claims miss.

Estimating the variance from the sample adds uncertainty, which gives the t-distribution heavier tails, and as degrees of freedom grow that estimate sharpens, so I'd say it approaches the standard normal and both claims hold.
The learning rate scales the gradient step, so the first claim holds, but I'd point out that a tiny step on a non-convex surface just settles slowly into whichever local minimum is nearest.

The step's size comes from the gradient's magnitude more than from the learning rate, and my understanding is that a very small rate moves carefully enough to avoid overshooting, so it eventually finds the global minimum.

Lift above 1 means two items appear together more often than independence predicts, a positive association, but I'd point out that high support only says an itemset is frequent, which is not a significance test.

Lift above 1 only signals co-occurrence above a baseline, which can come from chance or a shared confounder rather than a real association, and high support says nothing about significance, so I'd reject both claims.
The Markov property says the next state depends only on the present one, and an HMM assumes each observation depends only on its own hidden state, so I see both statements as accurate.

A chain's states can be defined to encode earlier events, so its future does depend on history, and in an HMM the observations are tied together through the hidden chain, so I'd call both statements false.
An LSTM's forget gate decides how much of the cell state to discard, but a GRU has only two gates and no separate cell state, so I'd say it is far from a renamed LSTM.
The forget gate controls what an LSTM drops from its cell state, and a GRU's update and reset gates do the same gating job on the same recurrent information, so I'd say the two differ only in naming.

Memorylessness does define the exponential distribution, but I'd point out that its hazard follows the density, which decays exponentially over time, so calling the hazard rate constant gets the first statement wrong.
The exponential's hazard rate is f(t)/S(t), which works out to lambda at every time, and I see that constant hazard as the reason elapsed waiting time doesn't matter, the memoryless property.
Covariance between two components doesn't depend on their order, so the matrix is symmetric, but I'd point out covariances can be negative, so the matrix need not be positive semi-definite.
Cov(Xi,Xj) equals Cov(Xj,Xi), giving symmetry, and for any vector a the quadratic form a'Σa is the variance of a'X, which can't be negative, so I'd say the matrix is always positive semi-definite.

A Bernoulli variable takes only the values 0 and 1, but since X squared equals X for such a variable, its second moment is p, and I'd take the variance to be that second moment, so p rather than p(1-p).
A variable with only the outcomes 0 and 1 is Bernoulli, and since its mean is p and E[X²] is also p, I work the variance out as p minus p squared, which factors to p(1-p).

I understand the Bellman equation as an optimality condition for the best policy rather than a recursive definition of a state's value, and Q-learning updates toward the greedy action, so neither statement holds.

The Bellman equation writes a state's value as immediate reward plus discounted value of successor states, which is recursive, while I'd note Q-learning updates toward the greedy maximum, not the action taken, so it is off-policy.

My understanding is that k-anonymity limits identification by sharing the decryption key among k authorized users, so the probability that an outsider re-identifies anyone drops as access is confined to that group.

If every record shares its identifying attributes with at least k-1 others, an attacker matching on those attributes can narrow a person down only to a group of k, which I see as capping re-identification at one in k.

Efficiency means the variance actually reaches the Cramer-Rao bound, and a minimum-variance unbiased estimator can exist without reaching it, so I'd call the first statement false while the second describes the bound correctly.

An efficient estimator has the smallest variance among unbiased estimators, and the Cramer-Rao bound is the floor no unbiased estimator's variance can drop below, so I see both statements as accurate.

Each K-means iteration can only lower the within-cluster sum of squares, which is bounded below, so I'd say it settles at the optimum, and the elbow method plots that same sum against the number of clusters.

K-means always converges, but I'd point out it reaches a local optimum that depends on the starting centroids, which is why people run several restarts, while the elbow method plots within-cluster sum of squares.

The negative binomial counts the trials needed to reach a fixed number of successes, as I understand it, not the failures before them, while its extra dispersion parameter makes it a standard choice for overdispersed counts.

Counting failures before the r-th success is a standard way to parameterize the negative binomial, and because its variance exceeds its mean, I'd say it is a natural replacement for the Poisson with overdispersed data.

Homoscedasticity means constant error variance across predictor levels, and when that fails, I'd say OLS gives noisy observations too much weight, which pulls the coefficient estimates away from their true values.

Constant error variance is what homoscedasticity means, but I'd point out heteroscedasticity leaves OLS coefficients unbiased; it distorts the standard errors and efficiency, not the expected value of the estimates.

Oversampling makes minority examples appear more often in each epoch, so their misclassifications enter the loss more times, and I see that as directly raising how heavily the loss penalizes errors on that class.
Giving the minority class a larger weight inside the cross-entropy changes the loss function itself, so I'd say each minority misclassification costs more without the data being altered at all.
KL divergence measures how far apart two distributions are, a distance-like quantity, and Jensen-Shannon averages the KL from each distribution to their mixture, so I read both statements as correct.
The KL divergence of P from Q generally differs from that of Q from P, so it isn't symmetric, while I'd note Jensen-Shannon averages the KL of each to their mixture, making it symmetric and finite.
I understand the error types as numbered by the decision involved, and rejecting the null is the second step of a test after stating it, so wrongly rejecting a true null is the second type of error.
I see a Type II error as a miss: the null hypothesis is actually false, yet the test fails to reject it, which is why its probability, beta, is tied to the power of the test.
